name.genre: county atlas and cadastral reference map
name.inspiration_notice: An unofficial interpretive brief derived from source research and intended to guide original map styling; it does not reproduce or imply endorsement by referenced institutions, publishers, or cartographers.

description.summary: A dense, commercially published cadastral atlas style built around township-and-range grids, section numbers, parcel boundaries, landowner names, roads, railroads, schools, churches, mills, farmhouses, watercourses, and occasional building or farmstead illustrations. The look is practical, local, subscription-era, and quietly ornate: a ledger of property and settlement wrapped in pastel hand-color, engraved linework, decorative frames, and civic booster marginalia.
description.design_principle: Make ownership, settlement, and transport legible before all else; every graphic decision should feel like an engraved county plate designed to help a reader locate land, neighbors, roads, and civic institutions on paper.
description.historical_context: County landownership atlases were commercially published, often by subscription campaigns. They developed from pre-Civil War wall-sized landownership maps and became especially popular from the 1860s onward, expanding from the Northeast into the Midwest during the 1870s and 1880s. Many volumes combined township cadastral plates with county histories, biographies, portraits, advertisements, and views of farms, residences, public buildings, mills, or prized livestock. Lithography, commonly with hand-color or printed color Engraved and lithographed linework with black ink as the structural layer Pastel hand-applied washes or printed tints for townships/parcels
avoid_misclassification_with: fire insurance atlas fire insurance maps: more urban, building-material coded, and insurance-specific
Rand McNally railroad atlases: more generalized transport/network-oriented
US Geological Survey topographic maps: contour/hydrographic survey aesthetic rather than subscription cadastral atlas
Pictorial bird's-eye city views: perspective illustrations rather than planimetric landownership grids
Modern parcel GIS maps: lacks hand-color, engraved type hierarchy, and atlas-page marginalia

behavior: Use color as light washes beneath black linework; opacity should generally sit between 18% and 45%.
Alternate neighboring townships or civil divisions with soft pastel fills; do not imply data classes unless explicitly mapping a thematic variable.
Let color drift and slightly overshoot edges by 0.5-1.5 px when simulating hand-color.
Reserve high contrast for ink, railroads, and administrative hierarchy rather than fills.
Use warm paper and darker ink to create most of the perceived contrast.

typography.character: A nineteenth-century mixed-type hierarchy: large ornamental display titles, Roman serif township names, compact serif owner names, italic hydrography, small caps for counties and railroads, and occasional script-like flourishes only for title/cloud web mapping platformuche use.
font_families: UnifrakturCook only for tiny decorative initials, not labels
typography.fallback_strategy: Prefer metrically stable, licensable fonts with the language coverage required by the map; preserve hierarchy when substitution is necessary.
rules: Prioritize owner names, section numbers, roads, and railroads over modern POI labels.
Use many labels; a slightly busy plate is authentic, but labels must remain locally decipherable at intended zoom.
Use abbreviations such as 'Sch.', 'Ch.', 'P.O.', 'Cem.', 'Sta.', and initials for owner names where space is tight.
Rotate labels along roads, rails, and streams; allow modest hand-set imperfection.
Do not use sans-serif UI type inside the map plate except for modern accessibility controls outside the frame.

required: Make ownership, settlement, and transport legible before all else; every graphic decision should feel like an engraved county plate designed to help a reader locate land, neighbors, roads, and civic institutions on paper.
preferred: Use dense owner/place labeling at high zoom; declutter by scale rather than omitting the landownership character entirely.
Style railroads as cross-tied or strongly dashed/double-line ink features.
Use serif typography throughout the map plate.
Do not use modern sans-serif map labels inside the atlas plate.
Do not use a generic modern street map as the visible base.
Do not use dark mode for the map plate.
For MapLibre/web map library, create a page container behind the map canvas and constrain the viewport to the map plate when possible.
Owner labels should be symbolized with zoom-dependent collision rules and abbreviated labels at lower zoom.
Create line-pattern images for cross-tie railroads and marsh hachures.
Prefer Albers/equal-area or local county projection for modern web maps unless mimicking a specific scanned plate; keep north-up and rectilinear.
On tablets, preserve the map frame and collapse directories/references into a bottom drawer styled as a paper slip.
On phones, require landscape for full plate view when dense labeling is central; otherwise default to a simplified township overview with zoom-to-parcel flow.

accessibility.color_independence: Pastel fills should not carry critical meaning alone. Pair fills with labels, boundary patterns, and clear legend text. Maintain high contrast for owner names and roads even if the antique texture is present.
accessibility.contrast: Preserve readable contrast for labels, lines, and critical symbols at intended zoom levels.
accessibility.minimum_text_size: Adapt historical or print typography to a practical screen-reading threshold.
additional: Test the compiled style in grayscale and under common color-vision simulations.
